newsitem.title: CONGO: Night curfew imposed in Brazzaville after clashes.
newsitem.headline: Night curfew imposed in Brazzaville after clashes.

text.p: Authorities in the former French colony of Congo Brazzaville put the capital under a nighttime curfew on Thursday after government troops clashed with supporters of former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
A communique broadcast on state television said the curfew would be in force from 7 p.m. to 6 a.m. (1800 GMT to 0500 GMT). Gunfire continued in Brazzaville's business district into the evening.
Witnesses said shooting broke out before dawn between soldiers and Sassou Nguesso's guards after troops in armoured vehicles deployed around his house in the north of the capital.
Gunbattles spread through Sassou Nguesso's stronghold in the northern suburbs and the army sent reinforcements. Four people were wounded, including one of Sassou Nguesso's guards.

Sassou Nguesso, interviewed by Radio France International, accused President Pascal Lissouba of surrounding his home with armoured vehicles and seeking an excuse to postpone presidential elections due on July 27.
"I believe that, on the whole, the authorities want to create incidents to prevent the presidential elections from taking place," he said.
Witnesses said at least six armoured cars had been deployed at about 4 a.m. in Brazzaville's northeastern Mpila district.
Armoured vehicles were on the streets in various parts of the capital later and soldiers wandered round firing in the air. The U.S. embassy advised its nationals to stay at home.

France has economic interests in the Central African nation and 350 troops there -- left over from an operation to evacuate foreigners from Kinshasa in the last days of the civil war in former Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Brazzaville is just across the river from Kinshasa, capital of the former Zaire.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting which killed 2,000 people following parliamentary elections in 1993.
Last Friday the government banned private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms, and on Saturday party leaders meeting in Brazzaville pledged to avoid violence.
Clashes between supporters of Sassou Nguesso and former president and prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango in their hometowns have killed 16 people in less than a month.

The government said it would pursue two senior members of Sassou Nguesso's guard it held responsible. A government statement on Wednesday night also threatened tough measures against anyone carrying an unauthorised weapon.
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. Frontrunners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and opposition leader Bernard Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.
Sassou Nguesso has not yet officially said he will run but he has campaigned widely since returning home in February.
Kolelas's supporters have made one southern, river-front area of the capital a no-go area for the army.

Sassou Nguesso ran a notionally Marxist single-party administration from 1979 until the advent of multi-party politics in the early 1990s. He then adopted an increasingly pro-Western foreign policy and liberal economic policy.
